Employee Stock Purchase Plans and the Burden of Substantiation: Tax Court Rejects Taxpayer Claim That ESPP Gains Were Included in Form W-2 Wages
sum: Moiseshyn v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-114, November 4, 2026

In Moiseshyn v. Commissioner, the United States Tax Court addressed a bit of confusion the taxpayers encountered when handling employee stock plan dispositions. The taxpayers believed they could defeat an IRS deficiency determination for omitted securities gains by asserting that the capital income was already embedded within Box 1 compensation on Form W-2, or at least that their employer’s guidance was so confusing their error should be excused. Writing for the Court, Judge Fung sustained the Internal Revenue Service’s deficiency determination regarding unreported securities gain from an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP), as well as omitted dividend and Treasury interest income.

The decision underscores the rigorous substantiation requirements imposed on taxpayers under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 61 and Tax Court Rule 142(a). For CPAs and Enrolled Agents (EAs), Moiseshyn serves as a critical reminder that third-party informational disclaimers—such as brokerage guides stating that ESPP income is “usually” included in Box 1—do not constitute probative evidence of actual wage inclusion, nor do they shift the burden of proof back to the Commissioner.

The taxpayers, Anthony J. Moiseshyn and Mai Moiseshyn, were pro se petitioners residing in California during the tax year at issue. From 1999 through his retirement in 2025, Mr. Moiseshyn served as a principal sales representative for Medtronic PLC (Medtronic). As a fringe benefit of his employment, Mr. Moiseshyn participated in the Medtronic Employee Stock Purchase Plan, an employee plan administered through Fidelity Brokerage Services LLC (Fidelity). Under the terms of the ESPP, eligible full-time employees could elect to contribute between 2% and 10% of eligible compensation to acquire Medtronic stock at an 85% discount relative to fair market value on quarterly purchase dates.

Between March 31, 2015, and March 31, 2020, Mr. Moiseshyn acquired numerous shares of Medtronic stock through Fidelity, establishing an aggregate cost basis of $57,498.37. On June 2, 2021, Mr. Moiseshyn liquidated these shares for total proceeds of $99,805.16, generating an aggregate gain of $42,306.79.

sum: Medtronic reported positive real-world registry results for two cardiac ablation systems on October 22, 2026, with findings presented at the Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society meeting. The company's Medtronic press release covered the Affera Mapping and Ablation System with the Sphere-9 catheter and the PulseSelect pulsed field ablation system.

Medtronic stock traded at 88.44 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 12:07 CET on Wednesday, November 4, 2026. Investors are weighing the clinical evidence alongside the company's portfolio shift toward cardiovascular, neuroscience and surgical businesses following the completed MiniMed separation.

The global APEX registry analysis included 1,050 patients with atrial fibrillation treated with Sphere-9 and the Affera system at 28 sites. Medtronic reported a 1.1% major complication rate, with no acute kidney injury, severe coronary spasm or phrenic nerve injury. Major complication rates did not differ significantly between first-time and repeat ablation procedures.

The REAL PULSE registry covered 1,160 atrial fibrillation patients treated with PulseSelect at 38 global sites. The analysis recorded a 100% acute success rate and an acute major complication rate of 0.09%, according to the company.

A separate European APEX analysis evaluated Sphere-9 in 46 patients undergoing treatment for sustained ventricular tachycardia. Acute success reached 87%, while estimated freedom from ventricular tachycardia recurrence at six months was 75%. Six major complications were reported in four patients.

Medtronic said the results reinforce confidence in the safety and performance of its ablation technologies. Khaldoun Tarakji, the company's vice president of science, research and technology for electrophysiology therapies, said the findings reflected encouraging physician response and real-world evidence across a broad range of arrhythmias. Felicia Kurz, vice president and general manager of Cardiac Ablation Solutions, said the company would continue developing care that is safe, effective and efficient.
The findings strengthen the clinical case for Medtronic's electrophysiology portfolio, but registry results alone do not establish a revenue forecast.

sum: Medtronic plc (NYSE:MDT) has taken a very different path from the broader market over the past year. The stock has declined by over 7% in the past 12 months, compared with a 17% gain for the broader market.

That underperformance raises a straightforward valuation question for investors: whether Medtronic has become cheap enough to compensate investors for the risks surrounding its business, or whether the market is correctly discounting a company whose growth remains uneven.

But before we dive into the investment story, take a look at our recently published article on Gilead vs. Medtronic: Which Healthcare Stock Offers the Better Mix of Growth and Income? for better comparative insight into the sector.

At $86.38 per share, Medtronic plc (NYSE:MDT) has a forward P/E of approximately 14.4, according to Seeking Alpha. The company raised both its FY27 organic revenue growth and diluted non-GAAP EPS outlook in September, and now expects organic revenue growth of 7.25% to 7.75%. That multiple does not look demanding if Medtronic can sustain anything close to that growth rate. More importantly, recent performance suggests the company is gaining momentum across several of its newer and established businesses.

That valuation does not appear particularly demanding for a medical-device company capable of delivering high-single-digit organic growth. But the multiple also suggests the market is not expecting Medtronic to become a high-growth company overnight. For the stock to re-rate, investors will likely need evidence that the recent acceleration can translate into sustained revenue and earnings growth. For a retirement investor deciding between Medtronic (NYSE:MDT) and Abbott Laboratories (NYSE:ABT) today, the question is blunt: which medical device dividend deserves the retirement dollar right now? One pays more today. The other has raised longer and compounded harder. That is the trade, and it deserves a direct answer rather than a split decision.

Abbott has the longer streak and the faster recent raise (the kind of 50-plus-year runway that put it in our free Dividend Kings guide, where we ranked ten of them by today's valuation). Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. At Morningstar, we think that the best dividend stocks aren’t simply the highest dividend stocks or the top-performing dividend stocks. We suggest that investors look beyond a stock’s yield and short-term performance—instead, choose stocks with durable dividends and buy those when they’re undervalued.

“Tempting as they might be, the stock market’s juiciest yields are often illusory,” explains Dan Lefkovitz, strategist for Morningstar Indexes. “High dividend yields are often found in risky sectors, industries, and companies.” And as a result, such high dividend yields can’t always be maintained.
Investors seeking durable dividends should instead focus on companies with management teams that support their dividend strategies and favor companies with competitive advantages, or economic moats.
“Moats signify a durable competitive advantage. Moats protect profits from competition. And profits fund dividends,” reminds Lefkovitz.
Investors looking for good dividend stocks to buy might consider adding undervalued dividend stocks with economic moats to their portfolios.

To find the best dividend stocks to invest in, we turn to the Morningstar Dividend Yield Focus Index. The dividend stocks on this list are among the index’s top constituents, have economic moats, and have Morningstar Ratings in the 4- and 5-star range as of Sept. 25, 2026.

Intuitive Surgical's Moat Is Getting Stronger. Is This the Closest Thing to a 'Forever' Stock?
sum: You may have come into contact with Intuitive Surgical (ISRG -3.35%) without even realizing it -- for example, if you've had a hernia repair or another type of minimally invasive surgery. Intuitive Surgical is the maker of the world's leading surgical robot, the Da Vinci system, which assists surgeons across many common procedures. This dominance has helped the company deliver earnings growth and stock performance over time.

Intuitive Surgical has an extremely strong moat, or competitive advantage, and it may be getting even stronger. This means the company may not face the threat of competition any time soon -- and this is excellent news for the earnings picture and for investors. Is Intuitive Surgical the closest thing to a "forever" stock? Let's find out.

So, first, let's consider the company's flagship product and its path so far. Intuitive Surgical offers the Da Vinci platform in four different versions, from a value-oriented product to the latest update, the Da Vinci 5. This latest Da Vinci includes more than 150 design innovations and 10,000x more computing power than the previous release. The new features offer strengths in areas like surgeon autonomy and operating room workflows. In the first quarter of this year, Da Vinci 5 placements totaled 232 -- that's up from 147 in the year-earlier period, showing momentum for this new product.

Intuitive Surgical's moat is particularly strong for a few reasons. Most surgeons have trained on the Da Vinci system, so we could imagine that they would prefer using this system, one they know well. The Da Vinci also represents a million-dollar purchase for hospitals, so once a hospital has committed to the platform, it likely will aim to stick with it to amortize the investment. Finally, a Da Vinci is deeply integrated into operating room operations, making it time-consuming and costly to switch to an alternate platform.

Now it might surprise you when I say that a new entrant to the market actually makes Intuitive Surgical's moat stronger. Medtronic won clearance late last year for its Hugo system for urologic surgical procedures. Importantly, Medtronic has emphasized that the Hugo may represent another "choice" for these surgeries -- so the company isn't positioning its product as a better option than the Da Vinci.

Medtronic PLC Stock (MDT) Closed Down by 3.30% on Jun 30: Key Drivers Unveiled
sum: Medtronic PLC (MDT) closed down by 3.30%. The Healthcare Services & Equipment sector is down by 1.48%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Boston Scientific Corp (BSX) down 1.99%; Unitedhealth Group Inc (UNH) down 0.91%; Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc (TMO) down 1.21%.

On the final trading day of June, the downward movement and elevated intraday volatility in Medtronic's shares were primarily driven by a broader capital rotation out of defensive sectors and back into growth-oriented areas of the market. Following a brief period where investors sought shelter in healthcare and consumer staples, a stabilizing global geopolitical environment and a rebound in technology and semiconductor equities prompted institutional managers to trim their defensive allocations. As a leading heavyweight in the healthcare technology and medical device space, Medtronic experienced institutional outflow pressures as capital reallocated toward higher-beta sectors.

This sector-wide pressure compounded the lingering market skepticism surrounding Medtronic’s long-term growth trajectory following its recent earnings report. Although the company delivered strong fiscal fourth-quarter results that beat top-line expectations, its forward-looking guidance for fiscal year 2027 fell short of the consensus estimate, prompting several analysts to trim their target prices. Furthermore, research updates during the month scaled back growth projections for the company's highly anticipated Symplicity Spyral Renal Denervation System, revising its expected annual revenue growth contribution downward. Investors remain cautious about persistent operational headwinds, including margin compression from recent legal payments and ongoing tariff pressures, which offset the optimism surrounding the company's product pipeline and surgical robotics expansion.

Additionally, the recent completion of the annual FTSE Russell index reconstitution contributed heavily to the stock's trading volatility. As index-tracking and passive funds executed large-scale portfolio adjustments to align with the newly reconstituted benchmarks, heavy trading volumes and volatile price swings swept through large-cap medical device companies.
